source: Cox & D'Antonio 3e Appendix D, PDF pages 554-559 (printed pp. 497-502)
about:
The forty-six rows of Appendix D, “Random incidence scattering coefficient table”, print over four pages, sideways on the page, in nine bold groups: sinusoidal 1D corrugation, periodic 1D battens, parallel V-shaped grooves cut into rubber sheet, periodic 2D blocks, randomly arranged 2D blocks, pyramids, V-shaped grooves in a 2D pattern cut into rubber sheet, wooden hemispheres covering, and vegetation with different percentage coverage of base plate. The columns are the one-third octave bands from 100 Hz to 5 kHz, and the values are random incidence scattering coefficients, dimensionless.

What the book says about them is one sentence, on the appendix title page (PDF page 554, printed p. 497): “Measured at full or model scale according to ISO 17497-1.” Section 13.3.8, “Scattering coefficients” (PDF page 512, printed p. 455), repeats it as “published scattering coefficients measured according to ISO 17497-1” and adds that “the use of the table values within a GRAM will take a little interpretation, however, as the scattering coefficient required in GRAMs varies between different diffuse reflection modelling algorithms”. That is the whole of it: no row says which laboratory measured it, at what scale, on what base plate, or with what uncertainty. This appendix is the only one of the four whose numbers were measured rather than computed; Appendices B and C are boundary element predictions.

Every row carries a bracketed reference marker, on the row itself or on its group heading, pointing at one of the seven papers listed on PDF page 559 (printed p. 502). Those markers are stripped from the name and the paper they point at is spelled out in attributed_to, because a superscript number is not a citation once the row leaves the page. Two papers contributed most of the table: Kim, Jang and Jeon (2011) the grooves and the twenty hemisphere rows, Yang, Kang and Cheal (2013) the six vegetation rows.

Twenty rows print no cell at 5 kHz, all of them hemispheres, and ten rows print an en dash there instead, which is a different thing and is kept as such. One cell exceeds one: the V-shaped grooves with N = 7 and P = 44% are printed as 1.17 at 1250 Hz, and a scattering coefficient above unity is what the measurement gave rather than a slipped digit, since ISO 17497-1 derives it from two reverberation times and puts no ceiling on the result. Seven cells are set without their trailing zero, 0.1 and 0.8 and 0.5 and 0.6 where their neighbours read 0.10 and 0.80, and one cell of the 20% holly row reads 0 where every other zero on the page reads 0.00. All are kept as printed.

The descriptions do not identify a row on their own. Under “Periodic 1D battens” the page prints “h = w = 10 cm, L = 2h” twice, once credited to Sakuma and Lee and once to Choi, and the two spectra differ by a factor of two in several bands: 0.28 against 0.44 at 630 Hz and 0.25 against 0.47 at 800 Hz, for the same design measured by two teams under the same standard. Under “Pyramids” the page prints “h = 30.5 cm, L = b = 2h” three times, twice with the continuation line “One in four pyramid corners raised from baseplate” under it, on two different pages and with different values, so those two rows cannot be told apart by anything printed beside them. The key of each row therefore carries whatever does tell them apart: the credited author, the continuation line, and, for the two pyramid rows that share both, the printed folio.
